common_name: Pink Rain Lily (Mexican Long-Tube Rain Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained sandy or loamy soil in full sun to part shade, where clumps will flush into bloom after warm-season rains.

directions: This eastern Mexico rain lily produces grassy, semi-evergreen foliage that stays attractive through mild winters but dies back in colder snaps. Its starry, rosy-pink flowers, two to three inches across, open in flushes through the summer within days of a soaking rain, each bloom lasting only a few days before the next rain cycle triggers new flower stalks. Give it well-drained sandy or loamy soil, since it tolerates drought between rains but resents standing water. It multiplies quickly into tidy clumps well suited to a border edge, gravel garden, or container planting, and divide only when flowering noticeably declines.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

planting.note: Plant small bulbs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to part sun, spacing them closely since this is a diminutive species.

directions: Native to Cuba and naturalized along Florida's Gulf Coast, this is one of the smallest rain lilies grown, forming a tight tuft of glossy, narrow leaves barely a few inches tall. Half-dollar-sized white flowers, often lightly flushed with pink, appear repeatedly through the warm season after rain, making it a charming edging plant where larger rain lilies would overwhelm the scale. It prefers well-drained soil and tolerates brief dry spells between waterings, and in containers it can be moved under cover during hard freezes to protect the bulbs. Use it along path edges, in rock gardens, or massed as a low border where its low profile and repeat bloom can be appreciated up close.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden
Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

common_name: Puerto Rico Zephyr Lily (White Island Rain Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, protecting from freezes where grown outside its tropical native range.

directions: Endemic to Puerto Rico's coastal lowlands and also found on nearby Caribbean islands, this rain lily grows shiny dark-green, linear leaves from a small bulb and sends up short scapes bearing white, occasionally pink-tinged flowers from summer into fall. It favors evenly moist, humus-rich soil in low-elevation grassland or forest-edge conditions and responds to rain with a fresh flush of bloom within days. In Gulf Coast gardens it performs best with part-day shade and reliable moisture rather than the sandier, drier conditions preferred by Texas rain lily species, and bulbs should be lifted or heavily mulched ahead of hard freezes. Plant it in a moist border or large container where its tidy, diminutive habit and repeat flowering can be enjoyed at close range.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation (IRC) floristic database
USDA Forest Service El Yunque National Forest plant profile
